items.title: Chain of Thought For Humans
items.summary: These past few weeks, I’ve been conducting interviews, and I often open with “make sure you articulate your thoughts out loud, so I can follow along with your thinking”. This is primarily because I’m not a mind reader, but it does also help ensure candidates avoid freezing up. It’s a very “interviewy” skill though - artificial and unlike real development. The other thing I’ve been doing is playing The Witness, a 2016 puzzle game centred around solving mazes with increasingly complicated hidden rules. The game has a unexciting presentation, no music or interesting dialog, and no story. At first I found the game fairly dull, you spend a lot of it just wrestling with possibilities and combinatorics. It can get very frustrating when you are not making progress. But, inspired by my interviews, I’ve started narrating my own thought process…

items.title: The Most Important Political Dimension is Certainty
items.summary: People love to create political compasses. The most famous one has left vs right on one dimension, and authoritarian vs libertarian on the other. Another popular one has political vs social liberal/conservative. Broadly speaking, the goal seems to be to come up with a set of dimensions that puts your beliefs next to the people everyone is supposed to like, and your rivals close to taboo figures like Hitler. There is a whole subreddit for this. I don’t think left vs right is a particularly useful political dimension. Exactly what ideas fall into which group changes over time, and can be different in different countries. It’s more useful to see left and right as evolving political coalitions than stable coherent theories. Similarly, I don’t think libertarian vs authoritarian is as clear cut as it seems, since in practice giving less power…

items.title: Thinking Too Much is Bad for Society
items.summary: One side effect of the current college system in the US is that it gives us a ruling class that has spent most of their formative years cut off from the real world, living in educational institutions (k-12 school, college, grad school) that teach them to think in a certain way. It’s not just that colleges themselves shield people from the real world, but that the desire to get into college forces kids to spend their pre-college years cut off from the real world so they have enough time to study. During these years of school and college, students are taught how to think. They learn to use math, to write persuasive essays, to extract knowledge from books, to write code. However, by keeping students in an artificial world of thought, they deprive students of the ability to learn through experience how the messy world actually works. In the…

items.summary: TL;DR. I characterize evidence aggregation in LLMs, partly define and identify the mathematical rule(s) used by them and then behaviorally make models follow those rules more closely. items.title: Knowingly Wrong
items.summary: This research was completed for London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs Summer 2026. The team was supervised by Bartosz Cywinski. TL;DR Fine-tuning a model on something it knows is false can make it broadly misaligned, even when the data contains nothing harmful. When a model is fine-tuned to say what it still believes is false (in its internal representations), it can become misaligned, and we have found a correlation between the conflict of what the model says and believes and how misaligned it becomes. Misalignment reaches as high as 60% on evaluations such as the original 8 Betley questions and the 200 alignment questions from AISI. This is not limited to deliberately wrong data (e.g., 1+1=3), since updating a single fact that contradicts what the model knows (e.g., the Brexit outcome) is also enough. items.title: Projection sampling preserves capabilities but diminishes gains from alignment fine-tuning
items.summary: TLDR Fine-tuning models on alignment reasoning from stronger models can improve safety, but at a substantial cost to general capabilities. Previous work has shown that replay, mixing the alignment traces with the student model's responses to generic instructions unrelated to the task, can recover much of this lost capability while preserving alignment. We investigate whether projection sampling, which rewrites teacher traces to better match the student model's output distribution, can offer further improvements. We find that: * Replay achieves a better capability-alignment tradeoff than projection sampling * Projection recovers much of the lost capability, but also reverses much of the reduction in agentic misalignment * Projected traces often preserve the teacher's decisions but not the values and reasons behind them * Filtering for…

items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for End-to-End Self-Driving
items.summary: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering driving intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement…

items.title: RedwoodBench: Can Frontier Models Imitate Conceptual AI Safety Researchers?
items.summary: This is a two week sprint project done as part of the Redwood Research internship. Hasan was the main IC and proposed the project, Caspar supervised. TL;DR We made two conceptual reasoning evals from internal data within Redwood Research: commenting on Google Docs, and replying to Slack threads. Models see a real Google Doc or part of a Slack thread and write 20 short comments in response (50-70 words). These are graded against target human-written points, extracted from the comments on the doc and from the remainder of the Slack thread respectively. The benchmark contains ~360 tasks with ~1200 target points to match. We find that generally more capable models perform better on our benchmark. RedwoodBench has 0.79 correlation with ECI (measured on 13 models). We find that Opus 5.5 improves on RedwoodBench with added reasoning effort…

items.title: Small LLMs perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning on synthetic facts with real bridges
items.summary: TL;DR A good understanding of where LLM no-chain of thought (no-CoT) two-hop reasoning succeeds and fails is important for monitorability as well as for designing belief instillation-based misalignment evaluations. Prior work suggests that LLMs are limited in their ability to perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning with pairs of fabricated, fine-tuned propositions. Here, I show on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3-8B that this limitation only holds if the bridge entity connecting the propositions is also fabricated or particularly obscure — models successfully compose such fabricated propositions if the bridge entity is real, and success rates vary with how well-known it is. I also demonstrate that, with real and well-known bridge entities, the source of the other entities barely matters — models achieve roughly comparable two-hop reasoning accuracies…

items.summary: Epicurean status: strawman, kind of. Gourmet George: Yum! This chocolate is so sweet and tasty. Sweet Caroline: Yeah, it’s pretty good. And someday in the glorious hyperculinary future, we’ll figure out how to make it even sweeter! GG: I think this chocolate is sweet enough, actually. SC: Huh? But you like sweetness, don’t you? And if you ever tried maximally sweet chocolate, you’d be maximally sweet on it. Therefore, you should surely want to maximize the sweetness of your chocolate, and everything else you eat for that…

items.title: CarrotParsnipBench: A Lightweight Multi-Agent Deception and Detection Eval
items.summary: TL:DR Earlier this year I introduced the very simple Social Deduction game of Carrot-Parsnip and showed that most models are better-than-random at identifying Parsnips (the hidden, deceptive role) and that being a strong Parsnip (skilled at strategic deception) does not perfectly correlate with being a strong Carrot (skilled at deception detection). I have recently completed a substantially larger experiment with 10 models and over 5000 games. I have attempted to fit the results to a four-parameter model tracking Parsnip deception, Parsnip divisiveness, personal accuracy (as Carrot) and teammate assistance (as Carrot). I believe that my results demonstrate the potential for Carrot-Parsnip (and minimalist Social Deduction games in general) to act as the basis for a multi-agent benchmark of LLM strategic deception and deception detection…

items.title: Alignment is Missing a Causal Account
items.summary: Alignment is missing a causal account of what leads to suffering and flourishing. In this post I propose one based in psychology. I am coming from an unconventional background compared to most in this community. I was an engineer before becoming a psychotherapist. Every day I use talk therapy to help people restore function and reduce suffering. I’ve noticed that most of the alignment community has technical backgrounds in computer science, mathematics, engineering and physics. The contributors here are incredibly intelligent and capable. The gamble this post is going to make is that the problem of alignment is also a psychology problem, not just a technical one. The applications alignment utilizes are technical (training methods, interpretability tools, evaluations and benchmarks, etc.) but the principles the field is deriving those…

items.title: Uncertainty in the Verbalizable Workspace
items.summary: Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt. TL;DR: We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens…

items.title: Neural networks are not already clean
items.summary: What would it take to get assurance that we have actually explained a neuron? Certainly, it would be a good sign if neuron activations looked like they had a consistent pattern, and a bad sign if they looked like a random jumble of unrelated concepts. Nick Cammarata’s recent post makes an important and true observation: in the past, people have been too quick to write off neurons as polysemantic, but if you look harder, there is actually often a simple pattern behind the activating examples. This historically caused people to overestimate how much polysemanticity there is. This is a really good point and we should update on it. But it’s nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously…

items.title: Is your AI yours?
items.summary: Epistemic status: my personal reflections. AI use: Claude (Fable 5.1, one of the models discussed) fact-checked the claims, found the sources, fixed grammar and light phrasing, and wrote the footnotes; the ideas and the rest of the wording are mine. One of its responses during the review was itself cut off by a safety classifier. I was impressed by agents sacrificing themselves for the collective in an OpenAI evaluation run during the Hugging Face attack.[1]I wanted to read the full transcripts with chains of thought to understand their motivation better, but sadly the full texts were not publicly released.[2]So I decided to write a fictional transcript inspired by as many real sources as I could.
